papers.title: Electronic Nicotine Delivery Systems Use and Reduced Days of Cigarette Smoking: A Causal Bayesian Additive Regression Tree Analysis of Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health Study Waves 4 to 6
papers.abstract: Background. Debate persists regarding the potential harm reduction role of Electronic Nicotine Delivery Systems (ENDS). This study estimated the effect of ENDS use on subsequent cigarette smoking days in the past 30 days among adult smokers. Methods. We analyzed longitudinal data from Waves 4 to 6 of the Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health (PATH) Study, including 4,909 established current smokers. Bayesian Additive Regression Trees for causal inference was used to estimate the average exposure effect (ATE) of current ENDS use (characterized as no use, some-day use, and daily use) at Wave 5 (2018 - 2019) on cigarette smoking days at Wave 6 (2021), adjusting for 26 covariates measured at Wave 4 (2016 - 2018). Results. Compared with no ENDS use, daily ENDS use reduced cigarette smoking by 6.17 days per month over a two-year period (ATE = -6.17, 95% CI: -8.16 to -5.29); whereas some-day use reduced smoking by 0.99 days (ATE = -0.99, 95% CI: -1.65 to -0.28). Compared with some-day use, daily ENDS users reduced smoking by 5.65 days per month (ATE = -5.65, 95% CI: -6.72 to -4.72). There was no evidence that these effects differed meaningfully across demographic or psychosocial subgroups. Conclusions. Among established adult smokers, daily ENDS use reduced subsequent smoking days compared with some-day and no ENDS use. These findings support the potential role of ENDS as a harm reduction strategy for adult smokers while highlighting the need for better characterizing behavioral patterns and health consequences associated with sustained ENDS use.

papers.title: Do Electronic Nicotine Delivery Systems (ENDS) Help Smokers Quit? A Causal Bayesian Additive Regression Tree Analysis of PATH Study Waves 4 to 6
papers.abstract: Objective. Observational evidence on the effects of ENDS use on cigarette smoking cessation remains mixed, partly because of potential confounding. This study aimed to estimate the effects of ENDS use on subsequent current smoking over a two-year follow-up. Methods. We analyzed longitudinal data from Waves 4 to 6 of the Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health (PATH) Study (collected between 2016/12 and 2021/11), comprising a cohort of 4,792 US adults who were current established cigarette smokers at Wave 4. Using Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART) for causal inference, we estimated the effect of current ENDS use on subsequent current smoking, adjusting for a comprehensive set of 25 pre-exposure covariates. We characterized ENDS exposure as no use (0 days), some-day use (1 - 29 days), and daily use (30 days) in the past 30 days. Current cigarette smoking outcome was defined as past-30-day smoking, two years after the exposure measure. Results. Over a two-year period, daily ENDS use substantially reduced the percentage of current smoking compared with no use (estimate = -15.7%, 95% CI: -21.5% to -9.9%) or compared with some-day use (estimate = -15.0%, 95% CI: -22.3% to -7.8%). In contrast, some-day ENDS reduced a much smaller percentage compared with no use (estimate = -0.6%, 95% CI: -3.2% to -2.0%). Sensitivity analyses indicated that the estimated effect of daily ENDS use was robust to moderate-to-large unmeasured confounding. There was no evidence that these effects varied meaningfully by sex, race/ethnicity, annual household income, sexual orientation, internalization, externalization, or age. Conclusions. Among established cigarette smokers, daily ENDS use, compared with some-day or no use, reduced the probability of current smoking. These findings support the potential role of ENDS as a harm reduction tool to facilitate smoking cessation among adults. Keywords: ENDS, e-cigarettes, cigarette cessation, Bayesian additive regression tree, causal inference, adult, Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health Study

papers.title: Structural Barriers and Socioeconomic Determinants of HIV-Related Mortality in Children Under Five: Mixed-Methods Evidence from the Child Health and Mortality Prevention Surveillance Program, Sierra Leone
papers.abstract: AO_SCPLOWBSTRACTC_SCPLOWO_ST_ABSObjectiveC_ST_ABSDeveloping equitable prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) policies requires local evidence, yet how socioeconomic, geographic, and health system factors jointly drive HIV-related child mortality remains underexplored in Sierra Leone. This study evaluated the association between socioeconomic status (SES), geographic access, and pediatric HIV-related mortality, while examining the system-level and sociocultural barriers driving missed PMTCT opportunities. Materials and MethodsWe used a mixed-methods design. Quantitative analyses drew on Child Health and Mortality Prevention Surveillance Sierra Leone surveillance data (2019-2024) for deceased under five years old (U5s) with confirmed HIV status. Stepwise logistic regression evaluated associations between covariates (SES, maternal education, distance to health facilities) and a composite binary outcome of HIV-related death. Qualitatively, 33 key informant interviews with PMTCT stakeholders were analyzed using thematic framework analysis in Dedoose. ResultsThe quantitative sample included 1,230 deceased children, of whom 162 (13.2%) reported an HIV-related death. Maternal education and distance to health facilities were statistically significant predictors of HIV-related death, whereas wealth quintiles showed no association. The qualitative findings identified system-level constraints disrupting the PMTCT cascade, including delayed entry into antenatal care, weak postnatal follow-up, stockouts of HIV test kits and antiretroviral drugs, limited polymerase chain reaction capacity and delayed results, and gaps in scheduling, tracking, and data systems. Donor-driven targets and funding constraints shaped procurement and service availability. Stigma, fear of disclosure, confidentiality concerns, transport costs, and poverty further undermined engagement and retention. ConclusionsPediatric HIV infection and related outcomes were driven by cumulative barriers across access, service readiness, and sociocultural context rather than household wealth alone. Improving PMTCT outcomes requires strengthening diagnostic and supply chain infrastructure, enhancing patient-tracking systems, and delivering stigma-sensitive, community-anchored care.

papers.title: Developing a Stakeholder-Driven One Health Collaboration Framework for Bovine Tuberculosis Control at the Human-Animal Interface in Lundazi and Monze Districts, Zambia
papers.abstract: Background: Bovine tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium bovis, is a neglected zoonosis at the human-animal interface in Zambia, particularly affecting cattle-dependent rural communities in Eastern and Southern Provinces, where cattle are central to livelihoods, nutrition, and cultural identity. While Zambia has a One Health Strategic Plan 2022-2026 and a One Health Secretariat under Zambia National Public Health Institute, operational collaboration between veterinary and medical sectors at district level remains fragmented, contributing to diagnostic gaps, under-reporting, and continued transmission through consumption of raw milk, undercooked meat, and occupational exposure during slaughter and handling of infected carcasses. The disconnect between national policy and district implementation has created a vacuum where frontline workers operate in isolation despite sharing the same disease burden. Methods: This qualitative exploratory study was conducted in Lundazi District (Eastern Province) and Monze District (Southern Province), Zambia, from February to June 2022. Ten Focus Group Discussions were conducted with 104 participants, including cattle farmers, cattle businessmen, abattoir workers, veterinary and para-veterinary professionals, and medical doctors, and ten Key Informant Interviews were conducted with District Veterinary Officers, District Medical Officers, Ministry of Health officials, and Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock officials. Participants were purposively selected based on their role, experience, and knowledge of bovine tuberculosis and One Health collaboration. Discussions were held in local languages (Tumbuka, Tonga, Chewa), audio-recorded with consent, transcribed verbatim, translated into English, and imported into NVivo 12 (QSR International, Melbourne, Australia) for thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke's six-step approach, with framework matrices for triangulation and trustworthiness. This methodological rigor ensured that diverse voices from community to policy level were systematically captured and compared. Results: Five themes emerged: (1) awareness of bovine tuberculosis, (2) socio-economic impacts, (3) public health impacts, (4) cultural practices and transmission, and (5) collaboration gaps and proposed framework. Medical and veterinary professionals demonstrated excellent awareness, while cattle farmers and abattoir workers showed poor awareness. Socio-economic impacts included reduced milk yield and carcass condemnation. Key barriers to collaboration included lack of diagnostic capacity at district hospitals to differentiate Mycobacterium bovis from Mycobacterium tuberculosis, siloed training curricula, absence of formal round-table coordination mechanisms, and limited funding. An existing enabler was informal collaboration in meat inspection between veterinary assistants and environmental health officers. Based on these findings, a five-pillar One Health Collaboration Framework is proposed. This framework was co-constructed from participant recommendations, making it contextually grounded and acceptable to end-users. Conclusion: Effective control of bovine tuberculosis in Zambia requires institutionalized One Health collaboration, moving from informal ad hoc interactions to formal governance structures. The proposed framework provides a practical, low-cost and contextually grounded roadmap for district-level implementation and is applicable to other zoonoses such as brucellosis, anthrax and rabies. Its implementation can help break the cycle of under-reporting and under-funding that currently sustains zoonotic transmission in rural Zambia

papers.title: Community-Based Hypertension Screening in Urban and Rural Zimbabwe: A Comparative Analysis and Implementation Lessons (2022-2025)
papers.abstract: Introduction Hypertension is a leading cause of cardiovascular disease and a growing public health challenge in sub-Saharan Africa. Community-based screening delivered through community health workers (CHWs) may improve early detection and strengthen decentralized chronic disease services, particularly in underserved settings. This study compared hypertension screening yield across phased implementation of a community-based programme in urban and rural Zimbabwe and documented implementation lessons for decentralized hypertension services. Methods A retrospective comparative analysis was conducted using aggregate programme data routinely captured in the District Health Information System 2. Screening outcomes from Phase 1 (2022-2023) were compared with those from the combined Phase 2 and Phase 3 implementation period (2024-2025). Trained CHWs used digital blood pressure devices to screen adults in communities and outreach settings, refer individuals with elevated blood pressure to primary healthcare facilities, and support follow-up. Phase 1 was implemented in urban districts and targeted adults aged [≥]40 years, while subsequent phases expanded to adults aged [≥]18 years and predominantly rural and peri-urban populations. The primary outcome was hypertension screening positivity, while secondary outcomes included participant characteristics and age-specific positivity rates. Results A total of 410,568 adults were screened, including 120,144 urban adults aged [≥]40 years in Phase 1 and 290,424 adults in Phases 2 and 3. Among participants in Phases 2 and 3, 76.0% resided in rural communities, 64.9% were female, and 44.9% were living with HIV. Hypertension positivity was 41.0% (49,276/120,144; 95% CI 40.7%-41.3%) in Phase 1 and 14.5% (41,972/290,424; 95% CI 14.3%-14.6%) in Phases 2 and 3 (p<0.001). Positivity increased significantly with age in both periods, ranging from 31.8% to 51.6% in Phase 1 and from 13.5% to 28.4% in later phases (all p<0.001). Conclusion Community-based hypertension screening delivered by CHWs successfully reached large urban and rural populations and identified substantial hypertension burden, particularly among older adults. The lower positivity observed in later phases likely reflects differences in age eligibility and population mix rather than programme effect. Scaling CHW-led screening may strengthen decentralized hypertension detection, although nationally representative surveys and longitudinal studies are needed to assess linkage to care, treatment initiation, and long-term blood pressure control. Key Words Hypertension; Community health workers; Community-based screening; Primary healthcare; Decentralized care; Zimbabwe.

papers.title: Human-Centered Design and Evaluation of an LLM-based Decision Support Tool for Nurses in Rural India
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform well on physician reasoning tasks, sparking interest in using them to guide mid-level health providers where physicians are scarce. However, evidence is lacking for effective LLM interfaces and their performance in real patient encounters. We report the human-centered design and performance of the NurseAI mobile app in rural West Bengal, India. Nurses participated in six design rounds that culminated in an audio-based mobile app that listens to the patient interview in the patients native language, suggests patient-specific questions for the nurse, and generates an assessment and plan. Physician graders evaluated the apps output for fifty real-patient consultations in the final version and found 90% of the plans were appropriate, 96% valid, and 94% safe. Several feature improvements have been identified for future versions of the app from the field use.

papers.title: Community Health Promoter-led responsive feeding for caregivers of children aged 0-59 months in West Pokot, Kenya (CHP-RF-WP Trial): protocol for a pragmatic cluster randomized controlled trial with mixed-methods evaluation
papers.abstract: BackgroundResponsive feeding -- recognising and answering a childs hunger and satiety cues without coercion -- is a World Health Organization-recommended component of complementary feeding, yet it is rarely addressed or measured in Kenyas community health system, particularly in arid and semi-arid counties. ObjectiveTo determine whether a Community Health Promoter (CHP)-led responsive feeding intervention improves responsive feeding practices among caregivers of children aged 0-59 months in West Pokot County, Kenya, compared with usual community health services, and to evaluate its implementation. MethodsThis is a pragmatic, two-arm, parallel-group cluster randomized controlled trial with an embedded RE-AIM mixed-methods process evaluation. Eighteen Community Health Units in two sub-counties will be randomized 1:1, stratified by sub-county, and approximately 340 caregiver-child dyads enrolled. The intervention comprises five-day competency-based CHP training, monthly household counselling and coaching visits over three months, mother-to-mother group sessions, pictorial job aids, SMS reminders and supportive supervision with fidelity assessment. The comparator is usual care. The primary outcome is the Responsive Feeding Practices Index (RFPI, 0-100), combining observed mealtime and caregiver-reported items, at three months after intervention initiation. Secondary outcomes include caregiver knowledge, attitudes and self-efficacy, minimum dietary diversity, meal frequency and age-appropriate feeding. The primary analysis is a baseline-adjusted mixed-effects linear regression with a random intercept for Community Health Unit, by intention to treat. Reach, adoption, fidelity and maintenance, with key informant interviews and focus group discussions, will be integrated by RE-AIM domain. Ethics and disseminationThe trial is approved by the Masinde Muliro University of Science and Technology Institutional Scientific and Ethics Review Committee (MMUST/ISERC/314/2026) and licensed by the National Commission for Science, Technology and Innovation (NACOSTI/P/26/4195285). Findings will be shared through publication, county feedback meetings and a policy brief. Trial registrationPan African Clinical Trials Registry, PACTR202611787801603; registered 9 November 2026; enrolment planned from 11 January 2027.

papers.title: Procedure composition, age and race/color in gender-affirming surgical authorizations of the Brazilian public health system, 2014-2025
papers.abstract: Hospital admission authorizations from publicly financed health systems are increasingly used to describe gender-affirming surgery, although they record billed procedures whose feminizing or masculinizing direction can be inferred from the code, without identifying people, self-reported gender identity or clinical need. This nationwide descriptive study examined the authorizations for gender-affirming surgery processed by the Brazilian Unified Health System from 2014 to 2025, which were selected from 3,888 public monthly state files of the Hospital Information System with a historically versioned classification of procedure codes. Of the 1,375 selected authorizations, 711 corresponded to directly feminizing procedures, 428 to directly masculinizing procedures and 236 to a complementary procedure that was analyzed separately. The feminizing share of the directly classified authorizations decreased from 81.7% (196/240) in 2014-2018 to 72.2% (213/295) in 2019-2023 and to 50.0% (302/604) in 2024-2025, proportions that describe composition within periods of unequal length and cannot be read as population rates. In 2024-2025, bilateral mastectomy accounted for 264 of the 302 masculinizing authorizations (87.4%), whereas bilateral breast reconstruction with silicone implants accounted for 118 of the 302 feminizing authorizations (39.1%). The median recorded age was 35 years in feminizing and 30 years in masculinizing authorizations over the whole period, and 34 and 29 years when the comparison was restricted to 2024-2025. The brown (parda) race/color category was recorded in 42.6% (303/711) of feminizing and 61.0% (261/428) of masculinizing authorizations, in a comparison pooled over the whole period and not adjusted for period or procedure. The number of hospitals habilitated for these surgeries remained at five from 2014 to 2022 and doubled in 2023. All aggregate results were reproduced by an independent pipeline that re-read every original public file. It was observed that the equal numbers of feminizing and masculinizing authorizations in the most recent period resulted from markedly different procedure portfolios, which suggests that the monitoring of publicly funded gender-affirming surgery may benefit from procedure-specific indicators and versioned code definitions, while questions of access and equity would require person-level and patient-reported data.

papers.title: Association between Social Media Exposure and Self-Medication Practices: Public Health Implications in Punjab, Pakistan
papers.abstract: BackgroundSocial media has become an important source of health information, including information about medicines. Exposure to medicine-related content may affect decisions to use medicines without professional consultation. ObjectiveTo describe self-medication practices and social-media exposure among adults in Punjab, Pakistan, and explore associations between self-medication frequency and demographic, social-media-use, and attitudinal factors. Methods: A cross-sectional analytical survey was conducted among adults aged 18-60 years in Punjab between March and May 2026. The final analytic sample comprised 280 participants. A bilingual (Urdu/English) questionnaire assessed demographics, social-media use and health-content exposure, self-medication in the preceding six months, medicine categories, and attitudes. The questionnaire was reviewed by two clinical experts and piloted among 30 participants. Descriptive analyses, chi-square tests, and multinomial logistic regression were reported using IBM SPSS Statistics; significance was set at =.05. ResultsSelf-medication frequency was reported as Rarely by 117 participants (41.8%), Frequently by 130 (46.4%), and More Often by 33 (11.8%). Fever medicines were reported by 179 participants (63.9%) and gastrointestinal medicines by 96 (34.3%); multiple-response medicine categories were not mutually exclusive. Instagram was the most frequently selected social-media platform. Advertisement recall differed across self-medication frequency groups ({chi}2(22)=35.28, p=.036). Belief that medicines shown in advertisements/posts were safe was associated with self-medication frequency ({chi}2(4)=14.26, p=.007), while perceived risk was not ({chi}2(4)=1.587, p=.811). The multinomial models overall test was not statistically significant ({chi}2(40)=54.07, p=.068; Nagelkerke R2=.205). Likelihood-ratio tests identified associations for daily social-media-use duration ({chi}2(2)=13.085, p=.001), age group ({chi}2(6)=14.930, p=.021), and perceived advertisement safety ({chi}2(4)=10.899, p=.028). ConclusionSelf-medication was commonly reported in this sample. Some social-media-use and advertising-attitude variables were associated with self-medication frequency, but the overall regression model was not statistically significant and the cross-sectional design cannot establish causality. Findings should be interpreted cautiously given the sample composition and reported data limitations.

papers.title: Impact of immune heterogeneity on antigenic evolution
papers.abstract: Antigenic evolution allows pathogens to escape pre-existing host immunity, but hosts differ in their immune histories because of population structure, demographic processes, and stochastic variation. Whether such immune heterogeneity promotes pathogen antigenic diversification remains poorly understood. We investigated how different sources of immune heterogeneity affect antigenic evolution. We developed a status-based multi-strain transmission model in which novel strains emerge stochastically within a tree-structured antigenic space. We examined immune heterogeneity arising from mixing between host subpopulations, aging, and stochastic variation in immune profiles, and evaluated its effects on strain coexistence and phylogenetic diversity. Limited mixing generated immune differences between host subpopulations, but increased phylogenetic diversity only under strong population separation. Aging alone had little effect on evolutionary dynamics but enhanced the effect of limited mixing on phylogenetic diversity. Stochastic immune variation promoted strain replacement rather than coexistence, primarily through variation in the overall susceptible population available to newly emerging strains. In general, immune heterogeneity alone does not necessarily promote antigenic diversification. Its effects depend on how immune differences are generated and maintained within the host population. More broadly, our findings highlight the importance of understanding how assumptions linking epidemiological and evolutionary processes shape the emergent dynamics of evolutionary-epidemiological models.

papers.title: The relationship between vaccination and preventive measures in case of infection and hospitalization: a cross-sectional study of Algeria using a Bayesian approach
papers.abstract: Response variables, in the form of categorical variables with numerous predictors, are often modeled using logistic regression models. A regression coefficient expresses the contribution of a predictor variable to the response variable through the parameter beta. Therefore, estimating the regression coefficient beta is necessary. The Bayesian approach is used to estimate regression coefficients in this research. The Bayesian technique combines information from sample data with prior knowledge of the characteristics of the parameters of interest to provide updated, or posterior, information. In this work, attention focuses on the COVID-19 epidemic in Algeria. We study the association between COVID-19 preventive measures and the risk of infection and hospitalization. Through this approach, we examine the role of preventive measures among vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals in relation to the risk of infection and hospitalization. This study determined that the association between barrier measures and infection among unvaccinated individuals was not statistically significant (odds ratio [OR] = 0.77359; 95% credible interval [CrI] = 0.55-1.05). On the other hand, barrier measures were strongly associated with infection among vaccinated individuals. An odds ratio of 0.11 indicates that vaccinated individuals who did not apply barrier measures had approximately nine times the odds of infection compared with vaccinated individuals who applied these measures. Individuals who did not apply barrier measures and were not vaccinated had approximately 4.65 times the odds of hospitalization compared with individuals who applied barrier measures but were not vaccinated (OR = 0.215; 95% CrI = 0.06-0.47). Among vaccinated individuals, those who did not apply barrier measures had 1.87 times the estimated odds of hospitalization compared with those who applied these measures (OR = 1.87; 95% CrI = 0.27-7.29). However, this association was not statistically significant because the credible interval included 1. According to this study, older individuals are more vulnerable when preventive measures are not strictly followed. Vaccination is also an important factor associated with reduced hospitalization, particularly among older individuals.

papers.title: The Impact on Clinicians of Recent Changes to the U.S. Immunization Schedule
papers.abstract: ImportanceWhile recent changes in federal vaccine policy may have negatively impacted clinician vaccination efforts, data assessing such impacts are limited. ObjectiveTo evaluate the impact on clinicians of these changes to vaccine recommendations. DesignA high-quality panel survey was administered in July 2026 and compared to a similar survey administered in January 2023. SettingThe panel consisted of clinicians from across the United States. ParticipantsRespondents included 508 pediatricians, 500 family physicians, 166 nurse practitioners (NPs), 167 physician assistants (PAs), and 166 nurses. Main Outcomes and MeasuresPrimary outcomes of interest included clinician strength of vaccine recommendations for patients and trusted sources of vaccine information and recommendations. ResultsMost clinicians trusted vaccine recommendations from professional medical organizations such as the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) (91%) and the American Academy of Family Physicians (AAFP) (90%), whereas fewer than half of clinicians trusted vaccine recommendations from federal agencies such as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) (47%) or the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) (42%). Compared to 2023, far fewer clinicians reported trusting vaccine information from CDC (47% vs 79%) or FDA (43% vs 75%) (adjusted p<0.01). Despite reduced trust in federal vaccine recommendations, most clinicians continued to recommend routine vaccines for their patients, with the notable exception of COVID-19, for which far fewer clinicians recommend vaccination compared to 2023 regardless of patient age, but especially among 12-15-year-olds (41% vs 71%, p<0.01) and 16-24-year-olds (43% vs 74%, p<0.01). Many clinicians also reported noticing substantial increases in the frequency (80%) and intensity (76%) of patient vaccine concerns over the past year, as well as in their time spent discussing vaccines with patients (61%) and looking up vaccine information (45%). Conclusions and RelevanceThis survey provides insight into the point-of-care impact of recent changes in federal vaccine policy and the shifts in clinician vaccine recommendations and trusted sources of vaccine information since the end of the pandemic. Professional associations can fill the current void in federal leadership by providing clinicians with reliable vaccine information and recommendations. Key PointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSHave the recent changes in federal vaccine policy impacted clinician vaccination efforts and patient encounters? FindingsThis large, high-quality panel survey found that many clinicians have turned to nongovernmental sources of vaccine information and recommendations as their trust in federal agencies has diminished. Despite this, most clinicians continue to recommend routine vaccines for their patients, with the notable exception of COVID-19. Clinicians also reported increases in patient vaccine hesitancy and time spent counseling patients about vaccines. MeaningMost clinicians continue to support vaccination despite fluctuations in federal vaccine recommendations, largely relying on professional medical organizations for vaccine guidance.

papers.title: Visual art for the prevention of student mental health difficulties in schools: Mixed-methods analysis of staff surveys and interviews
papers.abstract: BackgroundSchool prevention strategies are key to reducing the impact of youth mental health difficulties, such as depression and anxiety. Visual art programmes may be beneficial for prevention but evidence is limited. To better understand the potential for visual arts-based prevention programmes in schools, we explored staff experiences of using visual art for mental health and views on what is needed to facilitate successful programmes. MethodsWe used a convergent mixed-methods approach, combining online surveys (n=77) and in-depth interviews (n=27) from art teachers and staff supporting student mental health in UK secondary schools. Complementary survey and interview questions covered current use of visual art for student mental health, what a visual art prevention programme might look like, and potential concerns. We conducted descriptive statistics for quantitative survey data and reflexive thematic analysis for qualitative survey and interview data. ResultsVisual arts were seen as important for student mental health and commonly used: 65.8% of staff used visual arts to support student mental health in the last year, and 31.6% did so weekly, despite most participants reporting no relevant training. Theme 1, Art is a sanctuary in the school day, considered art as intrinsically linked to mental health, with art freedom conferring particular benefits. Theme 2, Resources in schools are stretched, represented the pressure of school environments, limited resources and need for prevention. Theme 3, Integration, flexibility and relationships as factors for success, highlighted integrating programmes into school practice, enabling flexibility and choice, and building positive relationships between students, school staff and external providers are key for success. ConclusionsDespite implementation challenges, visual arts-based prevention approaches were viewed positively. We recommend school mental health arts programmes should promote school ownership, include creative freedom, be flexible to schools and students needs, and be supported by both internal school staff and external providers.

papers.title: Knowledge of antimicrobial Resistance in Bangladeshi Caregivers of School-going Children: A Cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: BackgroundAntimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a critical global health issue exacerbated by inappropriate antibiotic use. This study aimed to assess AMR awareness and antibiotic practices among caregivers in Bangladesh. MethodsA cross-sectional design was employed with structured questionnaires administered to 225 caregivers. The survey evaluated participants knowledge of AMR, antibiotic usage behaviors, information sources, and socio-demographic variables. ResultsResults demonstrated a poor understanding of AMR: 78% recognized antibiotics as effective against bacterial infections, while only 35% acknowledged their ineffectiveness against viruses. In terms of antibiotic practices, 30% discontinued treatment prematurely, and 40% engaged in self-medication, primarily influenced by pharmacy advice (45%) or previous prescriptions (30%). Healthcare professionals were the predominant source of information (55%), followed by media (30%) and community programs (15%). Knowledge disparities were observed among socio-demographic groups, with higher awareness in educated, urban, and affluent caregivers (p<0.05). ConclusionsThe study highlights significant gaps between AMR knowledge and practices, particularly regarding antibiotic misuse and viral infections. It underscores the urgent need for targeted educational efforts, enhanced prescription regulation, and improved healthcare access to mitigate AMR risks in Bangladesh. Behavioral interventions addressing knowledge deficiencies and practical challenges are essential to combat this growing public health issue.

papers.title: Corporal punishment acceptability among university students without childhood maltreatment experiences: Associated factors and subfactor-specific patterns
papers.abstract: BackgroundAcceptance of corporal punishment and other harmful behaviors toward children may persist even among young adults without childhood maltreatment experiences. ObjectiveTo identify factors associated with the acceptability of corporal punishment and related harmful behaviors toward children among university students without childhood maltreatment experiences, and to examine whether these associations differ across types of harmful behavior. Participants and SettingAn online cross-sectional survey was conducted at four Japanese universities in June 2024. Of 699 students analyzed, 568 reported no childhood maltreatment experiences. MethodsParticipants rated the acceptability of 22 behaviors as discipline. Exploratory factor analysis identified three subfactors: neglect and psychological maltreatment, harsh physically aggressive behaviors, and less severe aggressive behaviors. Multivariable linear regression analyses were conducted among students without childhood maltreatment experiences. Higher scores indicated lower acceptance. ResultsMore egalitarian gender-role attitudes (B = 1.40, p = .001) and less frequent school-based physical violence experiences (B = 1.49, p = .024) were associated with lower overall acceptance of corporal punishment and related harmful behaviors. Associated factors differed across subfactors. Witnessing psychological violence, learning about child rearing, and enrollment in health, welfare, or rehabilitation-related faculties were associated with lower acceptance of less severe aggressive behaviors. ConclusionsFactors associated with acceptability differed across types of harmful behavior, even among students without childhood maltreatment experiences. These findings suggest the importance of prevention education addressing gender-role attitudes, recognition of harmful disciplinary practices, and child development. Educational opportunities throughout adolescence and young adulthood may help promote attitudes that reject violence against children.

papers.title: Targeted WASHmobile Program for Climate Anticipatory Action to Reduce Anemia during Extreme Weather Events in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
papers.abstract: BackgroundEvidence-informed anticipatory action is critical to mitigate the health impacts of extreme weather events. This randomized controlled trial (RCT) investigated the impact of the WASHmobile hygiene and water treatment program on anemia during extreme weather in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). MethodsThe WASHmobile RCT enrolled participants in Bukavu, DRC, from November 2021 to December 2022 (NCT05166850). Anemia was classified by WHO thresholds. CHIRPS data was used to calculate Standardized Precipitation Indices (SPI). FindingsAmong 1,208 participants, 68% (822/1208) were anemic. Extreme wet (SPI-1[≥]2.0) (odds ratio (OR) 2.29; 95% CI 1.03, 5.11), severe wet (1.5[≤]SPI-1<2) (OR 3.25; CI 1.53, 6.93), and moderate drought conditions (-1.5 < SPI-1 [≤] -1.0) (OR = 2.09; CI 1.28, 3.40) over the prior month were associated with significantly higher odds of anemia. In the standard arm, anemia was significantly higher during extreme wet conditions compared to near-normal conditions (78% vs. 62%, p=0.0496), whereas a non-significant decrease was observed in the WASHmobile arm (64% vs. 69%, p=0.55). Consistent with this, significant effect modification was observed between extreme wet conditions and WASHmobile delivery on anemia prevalence (multiplicative interaction p=0.044). These findings informed the design of the WASHmobile anticipatory action framework where pre-defined climate triggers activate an early warning system for anemia prevention. InterpretationExtreme and severe wet conditions and moderate drought were associated with higher odds of anemia. WASHmobile presents a potential climate-resilient intervention to reduce anemia during extreme weather. FundingWellcome Trust, UK government Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office, and the National Institutes of Health.

papers.title: Partitioning lifespan inequality in hierarchical study designs with an application to global healthy longevity
papers.abstract: BackgroundDemographic inequality arises from two sources: heterogeneity among individuals subject to different rates, and stochastic variation among individuals subject to identical rates. Partitioning lifespan inequality into these components has been limited to heterogeneity in single factors or, very recently, factorial study designs with multiple factors. Methods for hierarchical designs have been lacking. ObjectivesThe goal of this paper is to present a generally applicable method to partition inequality of lifespan (and other demographic outcomes) into components within and between levels in a hierarchical study design. MethodsThe analysis treats a heterogeneous population as a mixture distribution. Inequality is measured by the variance and partitioned into components between groups (e.g., geographical or economic regions), between sub-groups within groups (e.g., countries within regions), and stochasticity within sub-groups. The method is applied to global inequality in healthy longevity, using data for 194 countries from the Global Burden of Disease study, divided into four regions according to the World Bank income categories and into countries within each region. Results are compared for flat and population-weighted mixing distributions. ResultsThe protocol for variance partitioning in hierarchical study designs provides variance among regions, among countries within regions, and within countries. It extends naturally to multiple levels (e.g., states within countries) and to factorial components (e.g., regions defined by combinations of income and education). When applied to global healthy longevity, the dominant source of inequality is stochastic variation within countries, which accounts for 85%-95% of the overall inequality. The population-weighted mixing distribution reduces the contribution of between-group variance. ContributionSome of the largest demographic data sets have a hierarchical organization. The methods presented here make it possible to partition inequality, measured by variance, in such studies.

papers.title: From Policy Change to Program Impact: HPV Vaccination Coverage Following the Global Shift to a Single-Dose Schedule
papers.abstract: BackgroundSince the World Health Organization (WHO) endorsed single-dose HPV vaccination in 2022, many countries have adopted this schedule. However, evidence regarding the schedule changes impact on HPV vaccination coverage remains limited. Using a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, we assessed coverage changes following the schedule switch and explored stakeholders perspectives on factors influencing these trends. MethodsUsing WHO-UNICEF Estimates of National Immunization Coverage, we assessed first-dose HPV vaccination (HPV1) coverage among females in 49 countries that switched to a single-dose schedule during 2022-2024. We used Wilcoxon signed-rank tests to compare mean HPV1 coverage before and after the switch, stratified by country and program characteristics. We also examined country-level changes in HPV1 and complete HPV vaccination (HPVc) coverage across all 49 countries. We then qualitatively interviewed 33 national and sub-national HPV vaccination stakeholders from 15 countries and analyzed the data using thematic analysis. ResultsFollowing the switch, significant increases in mean HPV1 coverage were observed among non-high-income countries (55.0% pre-switch vs. 63.3% post-switch, p=0.019), countries in the WHO African Region (58.9% vs. 71.6%, p=0.038), and programs employing school-based delivery (57.0% vs. 66.0%, p=0.010). Significant increases were also observed in programs targeting females only (56.3% vs. 65.9%, p=0.040), those targeting single-age cohorts (61.3% vs. 72.0%, p=0.013), and Gavi-supported countries (54.9% vs. 73.2%, p=0.010). Stakeholders attributed coverage trends to multiple factors beyond the schedule change, including recovery from COVID-19-related disruptions, concurrent programmatic changes, and broader contextual factors. ConclusionAlthough coverage trends varied across countries, improvement in HPV1 coverage in resource-limited settings suggested that the switch to a single-dose schedule may have facilitated recovery from COVID-19-related disruptions. Continued monitoring of vaccination coverage, implementation outcomes, and program sustainability is essential to understanding the long-term population-level implication of the single-dose recommendation.

papers.title: Enhancing Access to and Utilization of Maternal and Child Health Service through Implementation of a District-led Integrated Mobile Health Service Delivery Model in Pastoral Ethiopia: A Multi-Method Implementation Research
papers.abstract: Introduction: Lack of access to essential health services has remained a significant public health challenge in sub-Saharan Africa. The conventional health service delivery models often fail to account for the mobility patterns and socio-cultural values of these communities. These communities are frequently affected by recurrent droughts, conflicts, floods, and disease outbreaks. This study assessed the contribution of a mobile health services (MHS) delivery model designed to improve access to and utilisation of maternal, neonatal, and child health services in pastoralist contexts of Ethiopia. Methods: A multi-method embedded implementation research with a non-randomized controlled quasi-experimental study design was employed in four selected Woredas of Ethiopia. Baseline data from July 2022 to June 2023 and endline data from July 2023 to June 2024 were extracted from DHIS2. The MHS delivery model was co-designed with stakeholders, redefined communitycentred outreach sites, and established a multidisciplinary team, that was implemented monthly. The average distance between the health facility and the centre of the targeted community village was 29.6 kilometres. Data were captured from routine health service records, MHS databases, and program reports, and 143 in-depth interviews among service providers and beneficiaries. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistical methods and difference-indifferences using Stata 18, while qualitative data were coded and analysed using ATLAS.ti. Results: During the twelve months, the MHS reached 79,404 people through 190 sessions held and offered an integrated essential health service in 20 hard-to-reach villages. In the study area, ANC use was 64.0% in Chifra and 75.6% in Dasenech. In addition, penta-3 antigen vaccination improved from 66.0% to 69.7% in Chifra and from 91.2% to 102.1% in Dasenech, respectively. In the difference-indifferences analysis, the MHS significantly enhanced access to ANC follow-up and completion of pentavalent and full vaccination coverage. A Woreda-led approach, community engagement, context-tailored and timely communication, and comprehensive service delivery by a multidisciplinary team enhanced the use and acceptability of the MHS in the pastoral setting. The contribution of MHS to ensuring access and use of MNCH services ranged from 13.0% to 19.1% for continuing family planning and antenatal care, respectively. Conclusions: The study highlights that the MHS delivery model is a suitable platform that has substantially contributed to improving access to and use of maternal, newborn, and child health services in pastoral, agropastoral, and scattered settlements. Being a woreda-led, participatory codesign, community-centred approach, and context-tailored health service delivery approach enhanced the acceptability and effectiveness of the MHS in reaching the underserved community. Integration of MHS with the existing PHC system, with an innovative, sustainable financing mechanism, is recommended to ensure access and use of MNCH in hard-to-reach settings.

papers.title: Predicting county-level opioid overdose mortality in Ohio through multimodal data: A spatiotemporal study using toxicology and EMS indicators, 2020-2024
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe opioid crisis is the leading driver of overdose mortality in the United States. While overdose deaths have decreased in recent years, the reporting lag in official overdose deaths presents a hurdle in implementing public health interventions to combat the crisis. ObjectiveTo address these data-reporting delays and improve prediction during highly volatile periods, we developed a Bayesian hierarchical spatiotemporal model using real-time drug overdose data sources to predict quarterly overdose deaths across Ohio counties from 2020 to 2024. MethodsWe implemented a Bayesian spatiotemporal model using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA). Rapid-reporting surveillance metrics, specifically urine drug test (UDT) positivity rates and Emergency Medical Services (EMS) naloxone administration events, were incorporated as fixed covariates. Models were constructed stepwise by first optimizing the spatiotemporal random effect structure and then sequentially adding fixed effects to minimize prediction error. A rolling training window was implemented and evaluated across different training window sizes. Results were assessed overall and stratified by county population size. ResultsWe found that the optimal predictive model structure consists of a two-year training window, a random walk temporal effect, a structured spatial effect, and fentanyl UDT positivity and EMS naloxone events. Incorporating these UDT and EMS data significantly enhanced predictive performance, with the most pronounced accuracy gains occurring during the unprecedented overdose increase associated with the COVID-19 pandemic in the second quarter of 2020. While predictive performance was highly robust in large, urban counties, predictive capability in smaller counties was limited by low data availability. ConclusionOur spatiotemporal prediction model successfully bridges the administrative reporting lags and offers near-real-time quarterly overdose prediction. The study also showed that integration of real-time data sources is especially beneficial for capturing sudden, volatile spikes in overdose deaths.

papers.title: Unmet needs of Polish patients with cystic fibrosis seen through the lens of crowdfunding
papers.abstract: BackgroundMedical crowdfunding allows for funding for needs not covered by the local healthcare system. We aimed to characterize the crowdfunding campaigns for the needs of Polish individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF). MethodsWe analyzed data from a leading medical crowdfunding webpage in Poland, focusing on campaigns for individual medical needs initiated between 2009 and 2017. We characterized the features of individuals with CF and the declared goals for which the funds from the online campaigns were intended. ResultsOf all 2,656 campaigns, 96 (3.6%) were related to individuals with CF. Approximately two-thirds of these campaigns reached their target amount. Individuals with CF primarily raised funds to cover treatment costs, medical equipment, and entertainment. The successful collection had a significantly lower financial target than unsuccessful campaigns. If the receivers were living in a city or fundraising to gather funds for an inhaler, these were also associated with the campaigns success. However, these associations did not reach statistical significance. ConclusionsCrowdfunding campaigns can be an effective funding source for the needs of patients with CF that are not covered by the public healthcare system. Analyzing crowdfunding efforts for specific patient groups can help reveal their unmet health needs.

papers.title: Changes in Health Behaviors and Correlational Patterns among High School Students Across Two Longitudinal Studies
papers.abstract: PurposeThis study examines whether six health behaviors remain stable among high school students across the school year and whether associations between these behaviors recur across assessments. Design/methodology/approachAs part of a school health program evaluation, a pre-post longitudinal health survey was conducted among two samples of high school students in a U.S. vocational-technical high school. Study 1 surveyed 114 students from late winter to late spring in 2024. Study 2 surveyed 177 students from autumn 2024 to late spring 2025. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests examined group-level behavioral change, and Pearson correlation networks described associations among six health behaviors: sleep, breakfast consumption, physical activity, nature exposure, social media use, and mindfulness practices. FindingsThe primary analyses detected no significant group-level changes in any of the six behaviors across either study interval, suggesting relative stability within these samples. A one-time survey may provide useful information for broad school health planning, whereas repeated assessment remains necessary for evaluating longer-term patterns or program effects. Sleep and breakfast showed the most consistent positive association. Physical activity and nature exposure were positively associated at three of the four assessments. Social media was isolated from the other behaviors at the first three assessments but was negatively associated with sleep and physical activity at the final assessment. OriginalityThe study distinguishes stability in group-level behavior from changes in the relationships among behaviors. The findings support efficient assessment for broad educational planning. They also identify behavior pairs that can be addressed together in school health education, including sleep and breakfast, physical activity and nature exposure, and social media, sleep, and physical activity. Research typeResearch paper

papers.title: Stigma and unsupportive disclosure reactions are associated with elevated depressive symptom burden among adolescent mothers in Juja Sub-County, Kenya: a community-based cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: Girls who become pregnant during adolescence in sub-Saharan Africa carry a high burden of depressive symptoms. Kenyan studies have relied on antenatal clinic samples and have not looked at stigma, the response to pregnancy disclosure and economic circumstances in the same analysis. We assessed how these factors relate to depressive symptom burden among adolescent mothers in Juja Sub-County, Kiambu County. We surveyed 227 girls who had been pregnant or given birth at 10-19 years, drawn by stratified random sampling from a line list of 466 mapped across five wards. Trained assistants administered a structured questionnaire covering background characteristics, pregnancy and disclosure, stigma, and a seven-item depressive symptom checklist. Elevated symptom burden was set in advance at four or more endorsed items. Two logistic regression models examined factors linked to stigma (n = 199) and to elevated symptom burden (n = 184). Of those with parity data, 194 of 197 had already given birth. Most respondents were 17-19 years old (86.8%) and single (69.2%), 92.5% had no income of their own, and 47.1% had left school early. Nine in ten pregnancies (91.2%) were unplanned, and 41.4% of girls met anger, rejection or indifference when they first disclosed. Stigma was reported by 43.2%, elevated symptom burden by 27.1% and thoughts of self-harm by 16.4%. Only 27.3% had attended any support programme. Being single was the one factor associated with stigma (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] 3.50; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.48-8.31). Elevated symptom burden was associated with stigma (AOR 3.21; 1.54-6.69) and with an unsupportive disclosure reaction (AOR 2.54; 1.19-5.41), and was less likely with each additional year of age (AOR 0.69; 0.49-0.96). Programme attendance showed no association (AOR 0.89; 0.41-1.94). In this peri-urban community, depressive symptoms clustered among adolescent mothers who had been stigmatised or poorly received when they disclosed their pregnancy, and stigma tracked marital status more closely than poverty. Screening with validated tools at postnatal, child-health and antenatal visits, guidance for families and partners on responding to disclosure, and community work on attitudes to unmarried motherhood deserve testing in this setting.

papers.title: Young peoples experiences of green social prescribing at a community farm and perceived influences on mental health and wellbeing: a qualitative study in Wales
papers.abstract: Mental health difficulties often begin in adolescence and early adulthood, yet most evidence on green social prescribing, which connects people with nature-based community activities to support health and wellbeing, comes from adult and quantitative research. This qualitative study explored how young people experienced taking part in a community farm programme in Wales and how they felt it influenced their mental health and wellbeing. Twelve young people aged 16 to 25 years took part in individual, semi-structured interviews at Swansea Community Farm in 2026. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis within an interpretivist paradigm. Four interconnected themes were developed: belonging in a supportive community; finding purpose through meaningful participation; personal growth and enhanced wellbeing; and nature as the context for wellbeing. Participants rarely described nature alone as responsible for feeling better. Instead, the farm brought together people who accepted them, useful work with real responsibility, and time outdoors with animals, and these were experienced together rather than separately. Participants had found the farm informally, and none had been referred through a formal social prescribing pathway. These findings suggest that green social prescribing for young people may work best when it is designed around belonging, meaningful roles and responsibility, with nature as the setting that makes these possible, and that evaluation should capture belonging, confidence and purpose as well as symptom reduction. They also point to the need for clear, youth-friendly routes into community provision, including self-referral. This was a single-site study, so it cannot show causal effects or represent the experiences of young people who did not engage, but it offers an in-depth account to inform the design and evaluation of provision for young people.

papers.title: Ni Binti Ni Mama: Participatory, human-centred development of a targeted nurturing care model for teenage mothers and their children in Kakamega County, Kenya - a mixed-methods study
papers.abstract: Teenage mothers and their children face multiple barriers to nurturing care, yet few models translate the Nurturing Care Frameworks targeted support level into practice for this group in sub-Saharan Africa. We describe the participatory, human-centred development of Ni Binti Ni Mama ( she is a girl, she is a mother), a targeted nurturing care model for teenage mothers in Kakamega County, Kenya. In phase one, a needs assessment combined a structured questionnaire and observation checklist covering the five nurturing care components (57 teenage mothers of infants), in-depth interviews with five mothers and five key informant interviews with health workers. Component scores were compared across groups using Welchs t-tests; qualitative data were analysed thematically. In phase two, a stakeholder workshop with the sub-county health management team and university experts generated and prioritised strategies; a draft community health volunteer training module was tried out with 21 volunteers. The mean overall nurturing care score was 69.1% (SD 10.3). Uptake of maternal and child health services was high (good health score 88.1%), whereas early learning scored lowest (40.4%): 28.1% of children had a picture book and 15.8% of mothers had read or looked at pictures with their child the previous day. Most mothers (75.4%) had skipped meals for lack of money. Responsive caregiving was lower among mothers reporting emotional stress (76.4% vs 86.0%; p=0.005). Interviews described economic dependence, absent fathers, family conflict, peer stigma and food insecurity. The resulting model, framed by Social Cognitive Theory, combines community health volunteer home visits, school and family sensitisation, teen mothers clubs and peer mentorship, lactation support for school re-entry, and linkage to youth-friendly services and economic support. Teenage mothers informed the model through their needs and preferences but did not participate in design decisions; their direct involvement and a feasibility evaluation are the next steps.

papers.title: Determinants of Tuberculosis Diagnosis Delays among Patients Attending Public Health Facility of Metekel Zone, Northwest Ethiopia, 2024 unmatched Case-Control Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundTuberculosis Diagnosis delays among tuberculosis patients can worsen infection transmission, disease severity, and mortality risk. Identifying factors influencing delays is crucial due to its persistence across healthcare levels and communities. The study identify determinants of tuberculosis diagnosis delay among patients attending public health facility of Metekel zone, Northwest Ethiopia:2023 MethodsAn unmatched case-control study was conducted in Metekel zone health facilities from March to April 2023, involving 210 tuberculosis patients (103 cases, 107 controls) selected through systematic sampling. Data collected through structured questionnaires and STATA used for analysis, including bi-variable and multi-variable logistic regressions. Variables with p-value < 0.25 in bi-variable analysis were included in the final model after checking model fitness and multicollinearity. ResultsOverall, 210 tuberculosis patients were included in the study. The following independent variables were associated diagnosis delay of tuberculosis: TB patients who travel greater than 10km (AOR: 2.941, (95 % CI: 1.509, 5.731); TB patients who are living at rural area (AOR: 4.135, 95 % CI :1.759, 9.723); TB patients who prior visit in holly-water and traditional medicine [AOR: 2.978, (95% CI: 1.292, 6.863); poor knowledge about TB [AOR: 2.826, (95% CI: 1.404, 5.687)]. ConclusionTuberculosis diagnosis delay is a major challenge to eliminate tuberculosis by breaking the chain of transmission. This study can be attributed to factors including place of residence being rural, poor knowledge about tuberculosis, non-health facility initial actions upon symptom onset, and far distance to health institutions. Recognizing these determinants helps in identifying and addressing barriers inhibiting early diagnosis, potentially improving healthcare access and promoting more timely diagnosis and treatment for tuberculosis patients.

papers.title: Long-term cooking fuel use patterns following a clean cooking intervention: Follow-up of the multi-country HAPIN trial
papers.abstract: IntroductionThe exposure and health benefits of clean cooking depend on sustained, exclusive use, yet few studies have assessed fuel use after trial support ends. We conducted a prospective follow-up of the Household Air Pollution Intervention Network (HAPIN) trial cohort to assess cooking fuel use for 4 years post-trial in India, Guatemala, and Rwanda. MethodsIntervention households in the HAPIN trial received a free liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) stove, fuel, and behavioral support for 18 months. At trial completion, control participants in Guatemala and Rwanda were offered a free LPG stove or alternative compensation, and in India, a free LPG stove and 18 months of free fuel. We surveyed 2,169 participants annually for four years on exclusive and any LPG use, examined post-trial use trajectories, and assessed factors associated with post-trial LPG use using logistic regression. ResultsDespite near-exclusive use during the trial, post-trial, few intervention participants used LPG exclusively (29% in India, <3% in Guatemala, near 0% in Rwanda). By year 4, 82% (India), 50% (Guatemala), and 10% (Rwanda) of intervention participants used any LPG. Sustained use was highest in India; non-use was most common in Rwanda; delayed use (starting years 3-4) was most common in Guatemala. Intervention assignment (aOR 1.8 [1.3-2.7], driven by Guatemala), socioeconomic status (up to aOR 40.9 [15.7-106.6] for Q4, relative to Q1), perceived ability to use LPG (aOR 3.9 [2.6-5.7]), household size (aOR 0.86 [0.79-0.93] per member), and country (aOR 5.4 [2.3-12.5] for India; aOR 1.9 [1.3-2.7] for Guatemala, relative to Rwanda) were significantly associated with post-trial LPG use. Only 27% of Guatemalan and 7% of Rwandan control participants chose an LPG stove (or electric, in Guatemala) as compensation, citing unaffordability and inaccessibility. ConclusionsA time-limited intervention, though successful in promoting LPG preference and sustained non-exclusive use in India and Guatemala, is unlikely to sustain the exclusive clean fuel use needed for long-term environmental and health benefits without policies supporting affordability and accessibility.

papers.title: Intimate partner violence victimization and perpetration with greater probability of brain injury in victims: A preliminary study
papers.abstract: BackgroundIntimate Partner Violence (IPV) can be either unidirectional or bidirectional. At times when it is bidirectional, the impact of the IPV would likely be greater in women compared to men especially in cases involving physical IPV. This study compared IPV victimization and perpetration characteristics and explored the relationship between IPV victimization and brain injury (BI) among women victims of IPV. MethodsIn this cross-sectional study, 23 women (IPV victims) aged 18-60 years who experienced at least one reported incident of IPV-BI were recruited from different community-based, women-serving organizations. Data collection included a comprehensive assessment of IPV, BI, and psychopathological comorbidities. The Conflict Tactics Scale-2 (CTS2) was used to assess for victimization and perpetration. ResultsThe participants had significantly lower scores on the physical assaults (t = 5.94, p < 0.0001, p2 = 0.62), and higher scores on the injury (t = 6.12, p < 0.001, p2 = 0.63) domains of the CTS2 compared to the perpetrator/partner. The physical assault scores of the perpetrator/partner were significantly correlated with the injury scores of the victim (r = 0.86, p < 0.001). Moreover, victims injury scores and their BISA scores were also significantly correlated (r = 0.69, p = 0.002). ConclusionsWomen victims of IPV, in contrast to perpetrator/partners, demonstrated greater physical injury, which were associated with an increased likelihood of BI in this cohort. Findings should be interpreted cautiously, as partners data were based on victim reports. Further studies are warranted to explore the possible occurrence of BI in perpetrators and then directly compare the injury exposure in victims versus perpetrators. Based on the findings of this study, it is clear there is a higher prevalence, as well as greater exposure, of BI and more serious consequences of IPV and/or IPV-BI on victims compared to that of perpetrators.

papers.title: Validity and reliability of the SSF Preschoolers' Activity Questionnaire (SSF-PAQ) for assessing active play, screen time, and sleep in Japanese preschool children
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe parent-reported Sasakawa Sports Foundation Preschoolers Activity Questionnaire (SSF-PAQ) is from a national survey of Japanese preschoolers out-of-preschool exercise, active play, screen time, and sleep. We assessed the validity, reliability, measurement error, paper-electronic agreement, and practicality of the Original version and explored a 24-hour version (SSF-PAQ-24). MethodsChildren aged 3-6 years from 10 conveniently sampled preschools wore an accelerometer for seven days while parents kept a time-use diary and completed the SSF-PAQ on Days 7 and 10. Criteria were accelerometer-measured physical activity (PA), diary-recorded screen time, and diary- and accelerometer-derived night sleep. ResultsThe concurrent-validity sample comprised 167 children (Original, 127; SSF-PAQ-24, 40). Original-version correlations were weak for organized PA and active play ({rho} = 0.24) and moderate-to-vigorous PA ({rho} = 0.29) but strong for screen time ({rho} = 0.83) and night sleep ({rho} = 0.78), which averaged 8.2 and 10.7 min/day above the criteria. Test-retest intraclass correlations were 0.78-0.96 for these measures and 0.27-0.89 for setting-specific items. Screen time was higher on paper than electronically. SSF-PAQ-24 activity correlations were not significant ({rho} = 0.17 and 0.06). Completion took 6.5-9.7 minutes. ConclusionThe Original SSF-PAQs main measures showed good-to-excellent test-retest reliability, and screen time and night sleep correlated strongly with the criteria. Activity-time validity was limited but comparable to that of existing parent-report questionnaires. SSF-PAQ-24 activity items need re-examination in a larger sample.

papers.title: Knowledge, attitudes and practices regarding antibiotic use and antimicrobial resistance among community pharmacy workers in Bukavu, Eastern Democratic Republic of Congo: a cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: BackgroundCommunity pharmacies are often the first point of care in low- and middle-income countries, yet the knowledge, attitudes and practices (KAP) of their workers regarding antibiotics and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) are undocumented in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). ObjectivesTo assess KAP regarding antibiotic use and AMR, and their determinants, among community pharmacy workers in Bukavu, Eastern DRC. MethodsA cross-sectional survey was conducted in April-June 2026 among 423 community pharmacy workers, one per pharmacy, selected by multistage sampling across the three health zones of Bukavu, using a structured, interviewer-administered questionnaire. Knowledge (8 items), attitudes (9 items) and dispensing practices (4 items) were scored using modified Blooms cut-offs. Multivariable logistic regression identified determinants. ResultsGood knowledge was found in 19.4%, favourable attitudes in 17.5% and appropriate dispensing practices in 27.4%. Overall, 96.5% dispensed antibiotics without a prescription and 9.2% knew the WHO AWaRe classification. University education and pharmaceutical qualification were independently associated with good knowledge [adjusted OR (aOR) 4.38 and 2.41] and appropriate practices (aOR 5.74 and 2.01). Good knowledge was associated with favourable attitudes (aOR 4.86, 95% CI 2.68-8.82), which in turn predicted appropriate practices (aOR 6.62, 95% CI 3.50-12.53). In addition, 57.0% knew of "Machange", an informal mixture of medicines: 99.6% of those describing its composition listed at least one antibiotic, and 65.6% of those familiar with it sold it. ConclusionsCommunity pharmacy workers in Bukavu show substantial gaps in antibiotic-related KAP. Stewardship interventions should combine education with regulation, diagnostic capacity and AMR surveillance within a One Health framework.
